subject: beetle
pitch: A proud stag beetle on a mossy log. A glossy chestnut wing case with a mirror shine, a black head and thorax, huge branched antler-like jaws in reddish brown, elbowed antennae with feathery tips, and six spiny black legs gripping the bark. A dewdrop clings to one of its antlers.
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module using the SDK to build a scene of a stag beetle on a mossy log, making sure the log rests on the floor plane with the beetle standing on top of it.

I'm thinking through the builder API's joint, chain, sweep, rod, part, and surface functions to construct the beetle's body, legs, and jaws, along with the log as a supporting prop.

For gloss on the wing case, since materials with fixed roughness are shared by color, I plan to give the elytra a unique color string so I can later traverse the built root and manually adjust that material's roughness and metalness for a shinier look.

Each leg becomes a chain spanning hip, knee, ankle, and toe joints, with roles tagged as "leg" for contact at the tip. I'll sweep a tapering radius along each leg chain for the geometry, then add spikes along the legs using base point, direction, and length parameters.

For the body I'm laying out coordinates: head near the front, pronotum at center, elytra covering the abdomen toward the back, all sitting atop a log. The log itself is scenery—a thick rod-like cylinder lying along the z-axis with rounded caps—built from a root joint even though it doesn't need articulation.

For texturing, I'm blending bark grain and mossy mottling on the log surface, combining noise-based color functions so patches of moss break up the wood coloring naturally.

For the dewdrop, I'll add a small glossy sphere with low roughness positioned near the antler tip, picking an approximate coordinate for now. For antennae, I'm planning an elbowed chain structure with multiple segments starting from the scape.

For the feathery tips, I'll skip texture cards and instead use several short rods angled from the tip point to suggest a feathery club shape. For the jaws, I'm planning a main chain beam with branch tines sprouting off at points along it, using rods anchored to frames pulled from the chain.

Now I'm working out the hinge setup — each mandible gets its own hinged joint at the head with a "jaw" role, and I need to nail down the exact joint API (parent references, aim/dir/up, role, group) before laying out actual coordinates for the head and body relative to the log's surface.

I'm building the mandible chain with jaw role joints and small rod tines branching off at intervals along its length, then setting up a mirroring function so I can generate matching left and right mandibles by flipping the x-coordinate sign per side.

Settling on jaw and wing colors to keep them visually distinct, then placing a tiny droplet detail on the jaw tine tip, attaching it to the correct bone joint name.

For the head, I'm shaping it from a scaled sphere with a dark color, positioned and sized to sit at the right spot, and adding small glossy eye spheres on the sides for a bit of character detail.

Now I'm building out the thorax as a lofted shape along stations with varying width and height, anchored to the body bone and positioned so its base sits just above the log's surface where the legs will connect. I'm then extending a similar loft down toward the abdomen to form the elytra, widening in the middle before narrowing again.

Without an environment map, metalness would read too dark, so I'll use roughness 0.15 and metalness 0.1 instead. Now I'm planning the six legs, three per side, each a coxa-femur-tibia-tarsus chain from hip to foot gripping the log, colored near-black, with tapering swept geometry and spikes added along the tibia.

Working out specific joint coordinates for each leg now -- hip, knee, ankle positions that splay outward and angle down so the feet land naturally on the log's curved surface.

Adding claw hooks at leg tips, then building elbowed antennae with scape, flagellum, and feathery club tips radiating from the last segment.

Now I'm placing the dewdrop on the left jaw's tine tip, using a small sphere geometry bound to the jawL2 bone for positioning. Then I'm working out the mossy log as a thick rod running along the ground, considering whether to use round or flat caps.

I'm designing the log's surface by combining a mottled moss paint for the top-facing normals with a wood grain bark paint for the rest, blending them with a conditional paint function based on surface normal direction, and adding squashed sphere clumps along the top as moss tufts.

For colors, I'm keeping the head and thorax near-black with a matte finish, and the wing cases a solid glossy chestnut rather than patterned, since gloss and roughness settings matter more there than color variation. After building the mesh, I'm traversing the scene graph to find meshes tagged by group name and tweaking their material roughness and metalness values for the elytra and dew-covered parts separately.

I'm assigning distinct unique colors to each part—dew droplets a pale icy blue, jaws a reddish brown, legs near-black—so each gets its own material instance without unintentionally sharing gloss settings across unrelated parts.

Now I'm placing eyes, mandibles, antennae, and leg joints with precise coordinates relative to the head and body bones, making sure parent-child hierarchy (log → body → head) and joint rotations default sensibly when no explicit direction vector is given.

I'm naming the leg chain joints systematically by position (front/mid/hind, left/right) and adding gripping spikes along the tibia using chain frame points for base position and direction, then setting up claw tips at the end of each leg chain.

For the antennae, I'm building feathery tips by branching several short rods outward from the chain's end point at varied offsets and angles, giving them a fan-like spread with a golden color and thin radius.

Now I'm defining the sweep profiles for the antennae and mandible—using tapered radius arrays or a radius function for the chain to get thickness that narrows from base to tip, making sure to pass color and name options to each sweep call.

For legs I'll use a similar tapering radius function, and for the log I'll sweep a straight path with a wavy radius function plus flat caps so the ends read as cut wood. Then I set up the thorax and elytra as lofts over stations with width/height pairs, shaping the elytra to curve down and sit just above the log's surface.

For the thorax I'm defining three stations that narrow slightly going back, matching color to black and keeping widths close to the elytra base so the transition looks natural. The head becomes a scaled sphere with modest segment counts for smoothness, and I'm importing THREE plus mottle, grain, paint, and noise from the SDK to start writing the actual leg array code.

Defining leg array...

Adding sweep, spikes, and claws to the leg chains, but I realize the leg tip at x=0.054 extends beyond the log's radius of 0.035 — the legs would be floating off the bark surface instead of gripping it, so I need to rework the leg positioning to keep them in contact with the log.

Let me just fix the numbers directly: log radius 0.06 centered at y=0.06, body center at y=0.14, and work out leg joint positions by computing where each leg segment intersects the log's curved surface at increasing x offsets, so hips, knees, and ankles follow the log's curvature down to its widest point.

I'll write a surfaceY helper function to compute the log's surface height at a given x, so leg points can rest properly on the curved log. I'm also reconsidering the log's length along z—0.4 might be too long, so I'll scale it down to roughly -0.16 to 0.16 to better fit the beetle's span.

Now I'm sketching the log mesh as a sweep between two endpoints with a slightly wavy radius, plus scattering small squashed moss clumps at computed surface positions so they sit flush against the log's curvature.

For the body, I'm checking that it hovers just above the log surface, supported by the legs, and nudging the body's y-position down slightly so the underside nearly touches the log without clipping through it.

I'm working through the leg geometry next—hip, knee, ankle, and foot tip positions—calculating where each joint intersects the curved log surface so the legs land naturally on the bark, and placing the head joint and sphere just above the thorax.

Now I'm plotting the mandibles as curved paths from the head forward and outward, then branching antler-like tines off each mandible with dew drops perched at the tine tips, checking that the tines sit above the mandible body for a proper stag beetle silhouette.

I'm sketching elbowed antennae with scape and flagellum segments ending in feathery fan tips, picking brown and gold tones for the antenna and fan colors, then setting up the jaw bone naming convention and elytra material before starting to write the final TypeScript module.

Writing module setup and metadata...

I'm defining the log's surface curve as a half-circle profile, then setting up moss and bark paint functions that blend based on surface normal and noise, and starting to build out the joint hierarchy for the log, body, and head.

Now I'm adding moss clumps as scaled spheres positioned along the log surface, then building the thorax using a loft across three oval stations attached to the body bone.

Next I'm lofting the elytra as tapering oval cross-sections down the back, checking that it sinks slightly below the log surface to sit naturally, then adding the head as a scaled sphere with its own eye spheres positioned symmetrically. I'm starting on the mandibles, mirrored left and right using a sign multiplier for their length.

Writing jaw chain code...

The dew sphere sits right at the tine tip, which matches the requirement that it clings to one of the antlers. Now I'm setting up the antenna chains off the head, deciding there's no explicit "antenna" role so I'll leave it unset, then moving into the sweep function defining their shape.

For the feather fan at the antenna tip, I'm building small rod segments radiating outward from the tip point, using a mirrored x-offset for left/right sides, and considering thickening them slightly to look like lamellae plates. Then I'm moving on to the leg definitions, setting up front/middle/hind leg positions with z-offset and spread values, looping over both sides to construct them with spikes and claws.

I'm checking that each leg's chain endpoints land correctly against the log's curved surface by computing surfaceY at the tip x-coordinate, verifying the front and middle legs rest properly on the flank while the hind legs' wider spread pushes their tips down near the log's equator, which still works since they're gripping the side. I'm considering tightening the hind leg spread slightly for safety, then moving into defining the leg's thickness sweep function.

Adding spikes and claw details...

I'm going through type-checking considerations for the leg chain destructuring, then moving on to a post-build pass that walks the mesh tree and adjusts material roughness per body part, like setting the elytra's roughness lower for a glossier look.

Checking a few remaining edge cases — material sharing per color group, the traverse typing, confirming `b.root` is called once and returned as the final Group — plus verifying the paint, noise, grain, and mottle helpers are all properly wired in, and chain/joint naming conventions are consistent across legs, jaws, and antennae. I'll wrap up with the final code block and a short note.
